title: Appendix A — Proposal
text:
Title
Downstream Effects of Redlining: A Case Study in Atlanta


Names
Andrew Lamb, Arun Waran, Bowen Tang


Project description
We are looking at disproportionate harm caused to historical redlined districts in Atlanta. We will look at factors such as green spaces, harmful industrial practices, food disparity, walkability, and other factors that would cause worse living conditions. Also how these districts have been economically held back.


Potential research questions
Where are there harmful industrial practices in Atlanta and does this line up with historically redlined districts? Who lives in historically redlined areas, and how is their quality of life? What are income levels sorted by redlined districts?


Inspirations
To bring light to the fact that historical inequity has present day effects, to show why initiatives like DEI are important and have precedence.


Potential datasets
To look at redlined districts in Atlanta we can use https://dsl.richmond.edu/panorama/redlining/static/mappinginequality.json. We could also use census data for income in these areas.


Communication plan
We will primarily use Google Chat for communication, members are expected to respond within 24 hours of a question being asked. We will meet at least once a week during the week, and if needed we can add a day on the weekend.


Project leads
Andrew - Tech lead, Arun - Point of contact, Bowen - Style lead


Conflict resolution/accountability
If a team member misses a deadline, the first offense will be a warning for the member and we will ask why they missed the deadline. After that we will report that they are not contributing to the group and will remove their name from that section of the project. If there is a 50/50 split we will get an outside perspective to mediate the conflict.


Implementation plan
Work is expected to be done a day before the due date (excepting the final video which will be made together), so members can discuss with the team before submission. By 11/5, each member will individually submit their writeup about effective teamwork and discuss w/each other. By 11/11, we will identify a model project from the list of examples and then record our expectations. By 11/15, we will have identified our final datasets and imported them into R for cleaning. By 11/18, we will have finished our EDAs and solicited feedback from one another to see techniques used. By 11/24, we will have completed all major wrangling and plans for visualizations, and set up a plan to implement it. By 11/28, we will have prepared a preliminary report to present. By 12/5, we will have finished a first pass on all of our analysis and write-up to edit together. By 12/7, we will have combined everything and made edits to present to the class for the second time. By 12/12, we will have incorporated edits suggested by peers and the professor to include in the video. By 12/14, we will have finished our video explanation and uploaded all deliverables to the Github repository.

title: Appendix B — Case Study
text:
Observations

The story unfolded through interaction

Small amounts of text at a time

The data source was quite clear, and the way it was split up into smaller sections (states) was informative.
Had both general info about each state but then also personal stories.

This added depth and breadth to the story which helped build a strong narrative. We saw both the human consequences of the restrictions as well as the concreteness of the policy decisions.

They also used the maze as another narrative device to make the reader feel the extra effort women have to go through to get an abortion, which made the whole thing feel very immersive. Oftentimes it feels like data storytelling can just be reading papers/sources and then indirectly tying them into visualizations, but this was not the case here.
The complexity scores do depend on how the authors choose to weigh the policies, so the mazes are illustrative and not direct translations.
For our project, we have a few takeaways from this story. It will be important to establish the question early, make sure our visualizations contribute to the main argument consistently, and use specific lower-level examples to make the patterns more meaningful.

title: Appendix B — Case Study
text:
https://pudding.cool/2018/01/chyrons/

Observations

The initial motivating examples (importance of television in modern media, concerns about partisan bias) motivated the need for the study very well
The story used very interesting visualization features such as triangles to compare with three different news channels. Each dot represents a word, which represents how frequent this word appears in that channel.
The way of explaining concepts is new, the most interesting part is the author highlights words and corresponds them to the graphs.

We could try and implement the highlighting words and when the cursor is over that work it highlights the corresponding part of the graph

The graphs change with the text


Data is clear, and it is from the Internet Archive. It was informative how they started
For our project, maybe we can use a similar graph technique to highlight the frequency of each variable, like how each variable relates to our topic. Also, we could organize our analysis around a series of increasingly specific questions. We can make each visualization raise another question so the analysis cascades gradually.
